blocks.x: You want to start over again? Okay. Yeah, I think it's doing, it's got it now. Okay,
let's get your full name again. Clarence Jules Ford Senior. Okay. And what's your name?

My name is Ted Jones. And my name is Dick Allen. And we've got it all hooked up to the hole now. Just making all kinds of noises. This is the first reel. And what's today's date? Today's the 12th? 10th of December, 1975. Yeah, on your watch. Oh, you've got a fancy watch. Okay, well. We can't afford it. All right. We've got as much as I want to get down
there. You start asking questions about that. Wait a minute, Dick. You just pay the cab fare,
all right? No, no, no. If you want, I'll ask some questions. What's your birthday? Where?
What's my birthday? Here in the Charity Hospital, December 16th, 1929. It's almost happy birthday, five. Yeah, in about another week or so. Six days. Six days. And you were born in Charity
Hospital? Yes. And we were talking about the musicians in your family before we ever had

the machine on. Well, far back as I know, my grandfather was a cornet player, Martin Gabriel. I was a drummer. And his sons, they all played, I believe. Martin Gabriel, I could call him Manny, my Uncle Manny. Uncle Clarence plays piano. Uncle Manny plays saxophone clarinet. He was a drummer with Louis Armstrong before he left New Orleans. And my Uncle August Lundwa, he married mine. He played bass. I know you know him. Uncle Clarence plays bass. And I was there, I have cousins. My Uncle had six boys and they all played. Charles, he and I started out together. He played saxophone, clarinet, flute like I do. He's in Detroit now. Which Uncle? Is this Manny or Clarence? Manny's a person. Manny's a person. Manny's a person. Manny's a person. Manny's a person. Manny's a person. Manny's a person. Manny's a person. Now, Uncle Clarence is sons. He doesn't have any musicians in his. He's the only one. And my Uncle Clarence, he didn't have any kids. But my Uncle Manny's the one that's more or less like a second father to the whole family. And my and our brother is like a second mother. Grandfather, I say, you know, she played also. Which I guess you know about that. But my Uncle Manny started me out. I believe I was getting ready. I was about fourteen. I was getting ready to be fifteen. Around this time of year. How it actually started. Charles. Charles was playing already. My little cousin. And I got a picture I can show you all. I'm taking around that time. Charles was blowing the clarinet. I think he was playing Sweet Sue or something like that. It must be 1944. And he said, I bet you can't do this. I said, I bet I could. So I took the horn. It was his father's horn. And I couldn't get a sound out of the horn. It was clarinet. He flat clarinet. And then as I picked up the horn, his father walked in the door. And I said, wow, I'm in for it now. Because see, my Uncle was giving us some whipping if we did something wrong. And he didn't get angry. He said, if you want to learn how to play, I'll show you. And so then Charles, well Charles was one of a fifty-five fifteen children. No, eleven children. And he was a couple of years under me. He was about thirteen at the time. Well, he didn't know me thirteen. I was going to be fifteen. And Charles would have to, being the youngest one, all the older ones worked and left all the dishes to be washed at the house. So when we'd have, I'd help him with his house. We all had housework to do. I'd help him with his housework. And then we'd get the, my Uncle said, we could use the horns after we, after the faster he finished the work, the quicker we could get the horns to practice. So I'd help him with the work. And then we'd practice. Practice over there. About his house. And sometime, uh, his mother said, I don't want all that noise. And we all lived around the corner where, uh, in fact we lived right now around the corner from where my Aunt Albert is living now on the mural. And my Aunt Albert said, I don't want all that noise. So we'd go, we'd come home, my mother said, I don't want all that noise. And then so we finally wound up in a chicken yard, where nothing but chickens would be back there and us. So that's what this picture that I'll show you. And we borrowed my Uncle's caps from the band. We both took it and put them on. And we both had E flat clarinets. And we played, uh, I must have played about six months. And at the time Mardi Gras came around. So it must have been in September, something like that I started. But Mardi Gras came around and he said, uh, get you a job for carnival. And, uh, I didn't know about three tunes because we were learning. We would, we would, we would, we would force that system that my Uncle used. He would learn home sweet home first, which is similar to a scale. And then he'd write out the C scale, then the F scale. And then, uh, well, I, I know it, I knew that, uh, an eighth note got a half a beat and a quarter note got one beat. So, uh, with that I tried to buy some little sheet music and learn tunes, which, the tunes that they were playing in this particular Mardi Gras parade were, like, Who Drew the Whiskey in the Well, Lady Be Good, I believe, When the Saints Go Marching In. Yeah, those three. I can remember. And, uh, my Uncle was supposed to work, but he, people called him, so he said he'd send me, he sent Charles with another, this was the Eureka band that I wanted. I don't believe Sheep was with him at the time. But I remember Kid Shots was in the band, and T-Boy Ray Me was the leader of the band. I remember that. And that was my first professional engagement. That Mardi Gras? That Mardi Gras 19, I believe if there was a Mardi Gras in 45, I'm not sure. Because, see, they cut it out from the wall. I don't know what year. They'd stop Mardi Gras tomorrow? Yeah. I don't know how many years they cut it out. They may have stopped it for two years or three years. But, uh, the first one after, uh, it was the first one after they stopped it. And I don't know if they stopped it in 45, and they started again in 45 rather. Or 45, I believe it was 45. Well, 15. That would have been your first engagement. My first time I meet him. Did you get paid for it? I got 15 dollars. I'll never forget. Wow. Most of mine I never had in my life. That's right. That was a lot, wasn't it? Yeah, but we walked eight hours. Yeah. We walked eight hours. We'd had to walk. And, uh, I was so tired, I couldn't walk and my mouth was so sore. And you kept playing those same three, Terrence? Well, we played those three and the others would be maybe something real easy to catch, something like that. But I remember those three. Something you could improvise really. Yes. And I may have played one or two others, but I don't know. Oh, Panama was another one. Panama too. But when I learned Panama, I didn't learn the whole thing like they do it now. And, uh, just the da-da-da-da-da-da, that's the fault I learned my uncle talking, because it would have been too much trouble to learn that. Mm-hmm. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da, all I'd like I knew it now. But that was E flat climbing. So I said, I started in jazz with Dixonland, and went all the way up to bebop and other things, and then went back to Dixonland. So you've gone. Yeah. I made a cycle. But that was the first job I played for money, period. And the second one was with the Adams family. We kid about that now. With the Placide and Justin? Yeah, their family. They had a family group. The mother played piano. Placide played drums at the time, yeah. Yeah, we played great drums. Uh-huh. And Justin, and Gerald, Gerald played bass. Gerald right now is not active in music. He just gave it up for a while. I guess he would play a game sometime. But Gerald, he's not there, I don't believe he's fifty years old. He's about forty-seven. Because Gerald was a couple of years old. I remember I'm forty-five. Placide and I are the same age. About a few months different. And that was the second job, and I played so bad until they said they wanted somebody to play a little better. Where were you at? Where'd you play? Over the river. In, I believe it was the Moulin Rouge. The Rouge? Yeah. See, at that time, they was working in Algiers and Gretna. There was more work there than it was in the Allers.
Yeah, I heard, I think, that, uh, a lot of people played across the river.

Yeah, I'd get the ferry. Ferry was in Nicola Dimes. You know, Algiers, in the All Street. Nicola Dimes. And then you got, you could catch a bus after you got over there. The whole thing was about twenty-five cents maybe at the most, because coffee was seventeen cents. And you got a, and a bus over there was, I'd say fifty cents was your round trip. You could make it. You could catch another bus over there and the bus would go to Gretna or Marrero, I'm not sure.
And Moulin Rouge was right on, right near Barataria Boulevard. Well, it's. In Marrero. Yeah, well, in Marrero. I used to go there.

Yeah, yeah, well, that was in the forties. Yeah, in the later years. And, uh, I believe that was the place, because I was new to this and I was excited and I barely could, I could barely could play. Oh, I hear the phone. We need to catch it. We can stop.
We can stop. Yeah? All right? Yeah, that's all right. Okay, we're starting.
You want to hear a bit of it? No, wait, no. Not necessarily. Okay, we can go. Because I don't like the sound of my voice. Oh, well, let's see, that's what I, that's what I, that's what I.
See, wait, you, you said there were a lot of, what other clubs were across the river?

Uh, the Moulin Rouge was one, I remember, I remember, I believe it was called Specs or something. Mm-hmm, yeah. Specs was on the air. And there was a Moonlight Inn. Yeah. That's, those two I remember. Mm-hmm. Because one of them had a windmill. Well, that's the Moulin Rouge. Oh, okay. Yeah, I see. Specs had glasses. It seemed like it was. But it was, uh, um, uh, a windmill was a neon lighted windmill. Mm-hmm. I remember that much, because it was the first excitement of the first time playing indoors. And I played clarinet, all I had was a clarinet. The way I got this clarinet, well, my uncle used to lend me his clarinet. But my godmother, who raised my mother, we used to call her in the name Creole, she had a, her mother had a clarinet that was kept from her husband for maybe, let's see, it was 1944 or 45. He died in 1915 or something like that. And he used to play the clarinet when he was young. And he died, and he kept that clarinet. And it was, all that time, the keys wouldn't move. So when I got it, my uncle, man, he fixed it up and made it away. He bought the parts from Peterson, who all musicians used to go by at that time. Pete Fong used to live around the corner from there. And put it together, and it was the first client that I had on my own. Didn't have a case. I think my mother made a bag out of flour sack bags or something like that. And I was, I would go to the little jobs I had with that client. I felt like I had a million dollars, because the first time I had an instrument of my own. It was the Albert system, which I now played the BM system, or the Boyum system, which is the correct pronunciation.
What's the difference? Or is it?

The difference in the Albert system is the old original system, or Louis Cantrell plays the Albert system, Willie Humphrey plays it. The only ones that play the other, or George Lewis play the Albert system. The ones that, it's an improved system. The newer system is Boyum or it's improved. It's a little different. It's closer to the saxophone. It's two notes different. But it's used more or less a symphony orchestra. When it's in B flat.
It's a difference in the fingering? Or?

Yes, the fingering. The fingering, you make F1 a different way. You make B flat a different way. You make C a different way. Those three notes. And on the new improved system, you can make one note two different ways. Whereas on the Albert system, you learned it one way, and you made it that one way. Was the tone different? The tone, I think, is bigger on the Albert system. It's better for jazz. Because it has a more mellow, more jazzy sound. Whereas the Boyum system has, like Benny Goodman has the Boyum system. He has the more refined sound. Symphony orchestra players use the new system. But at the time, I was, well that's what I was taught and that's what I learned it.
And with the system, the newer system, is your speed quicker?

Well, yes. Any quicker? Yes, it's quicker after you learn. But there are guys that play there, like Barney Beaker and all of them, that play at Albert system just as fast as anybody could play the other. It's a matter of what you have. It's a matter of what you have, you use it. I thought Jimmy Nunez is fast as a player. He played it, too. He played the Albert system. Yeah, well he played the Albert system. But I used the girl.
They all play improved. They all play improved with that extra key for your… Improved Albert. Yeah, for your right little finger.

But I've never seen an improved Albert. I believe Irvin Fazola played one, too. George Lewis, yeah. Some people. Well, they made them during the last ones that they made. I guess the last ones they made were in the 30s. Now, right now, Lloyd Cottrell has a new one. But it's not an improved one. It's just a player. But it's a new one that was given to him by the Selma people.
Must be special on it.

It's very… Now, I tried it. I hadn't played one in twenty years and I tried it. And it played so good. The sound was so good. I said if I could get another one like that I'd go back to playing the Albert system. It's such a good tone that was in the clarinet. But after I got this clarinet, well, I would just try to play it first thing in the morning, the last thing at night. Because I just wanted to play music and that was a great thing in my life. And while I started working after, I believe in World War II ended, I got a job. I was waiting in the drugstore. And I wanted to play saxophone also because the clarinet players at the time were, people wanted the saxophone. They didn't want a clarinet player. I mean, which I wasn't a good clarinet player anyway, but they said I wanted the saxophone.
Well, was this because most of the music, the pop music?

The music was coming out for saxophone. The clarinet was like a thing of the past, you know. And the guys wanted to, I wanted to saxophone. And if you were just going to play clarinet it would have been more of a Dixieland. I would have had the more of a Dixieland. That's all. And there weren't too many jobs and the Dixieland players, they had many of them. They had too many players for the work, I don't mind. Because every one of them was, George Lewis was working on the riverfront and Willie Humphrey was doing something else, collecting insurance. They couldn't make a living at it. But if you played in a nightclub, you know, six nights a week you could play alto sax and maybe double on the clarinet and make a living. Which my uncle played saxophone too, but clarinet was the start because it makes you a better saxophone player. Do you think it does? Which I know it does, even today. Well how does it- Because it's harder. It's a harder instrument to learn so when you get to the saxophone it's- Yeah, you fly over it in a sense. It's what all saxophonists start out on them, most of them. Now if you want to learn to play clarinet after you play saxophone, it's harder. Whereas if you start out playing clarinet, go to saxophone, it's better. You learn to play saxophone and you still can retain the ability you have on the clarinet. Even if you don't play it, you can go back to it and catch up where you left off. But if you never play the clarinet, it's harder. And there's one guy that did that well, Emmanuel Gusto, he learned to play clarinet. And after he was, when he was almost 50 years old, around that age, and he plays very well now, but he didn't play clarinet at all. He played trumpet. And he learned to play saxophone later. And then when he got late in life, the work was for clarinet, so he started playing clarinet and he learned to play it. That's what he's playing now, clarinet right now. And anyway, so I got a, I bought, my mother signed for me to get a saxophone and wear lines, free saxophone I ever had was alto sax, kind.
What's the band then, you'd have what, two, two tenets? What do you mean, a saxophone? It was a big band.

It was a big band. It was a big band. Well, there was four or five saxophones. But four saxophones, I'd say, three trumpets and a trombone. Some would have two trumpets, it was a small band, but at that time, like Herbert Liris' band, I used, my uncle August was playing with them and he'd bring me around just to be around the musicians and listen at the band. Even before I was playing music, when I was thirteen, thirteen years old. I remember because they had four saxophones and they had three trumpets and two trombones. And they had four rhythm. You'd have an alto? They had two altos, two tenets. Two tenets. They had three trumpets, two trombones. And that band sounded like the greatest band in the world, I mean. Because I used to listen to Carol Levine, he was playing alto, lead alto sax and clarinet, and he was very good. But they played more of the stuff that Harry James and Convases did. And that band was Swing? Swing. It was Swing. It was Swing band. Duke Ellington. And they had a book, I mean it's this thick, arrangements. And that's when I said, well I want to learn how to read music because I just wanted to play in that band, in a band like that anyway. And when I was a senior in high school I was in a band, the whole band, Booker T. Washington, I was in a school band playing clarinet in the marches. There was Joe Jones, I don't know, you must know him. Merman? Yes. He was there when Melvin's funeral, when Melvin died. Melvin was in that band, that's where I, Melvin was at Booker T. Washington High School also.
Melvin Lastic.

Yeah. And he and I were in Booker T. Washington's band, and we made up, all of Booker T. Washington's band made up a swing band. We got Hogan, he was dead, a drummer. He didn't have a set of drums. He had to borrow a bass drum from somebody, and he had a snare drum, stands. And I had alto sax and another guy named Fuzzy, he was playing alto, he was in the band also. Who's that? Melvin Lastic. Louis Sergin is his name, he's not in New Orleans now, he went to California. But he and I played alto sax. Joe Jones was a piano player. And which he later on made a rock and roll hit you talk too much. He does talk too much. But at this time he was just going to school. He wasn't in the band, because they didn't use the piano. He was a veteran that came back from the Navy and was going to school on the GI Bill. Sheik was going there too around that time. He was an older guy but he was going to Booker T. Washington. And that's where I first met him. And so we got up a school band together and we played. We got some arrangements, some stop arrangements. And we started playing the voices. The first job we played was, one of them was Corpus Christi used to let us use the auditorium rehearsal. And we used to walk up there from Booker T. Washington to Corpus Christi every day. And that's a good way. All the guys, we used to leave Booker T. Washington, I used to go home first and meet him at 6 o'clock. And we'd be down there every day we'd rehearse. Because Dukey Chase had a band and we wanted to be as good a band as Dukey Chase, because we were the number two band, which we didn't get the name that they did. Well he had the better players and all. But he had a good band. But later on the band built up until the guys got out of school, which was Joe Jones, was the first big band I played. And after I played with the Adams, one of the first jobs I played when I got to saxophone was with Sheik. I'd say about the second job I played indoors. Because he was playing the Sheik of Arabita and as simple as it is I didn't know it. So my uncle had sent one of his sons, Martin, to play also with two trumpets and one saxophone, which was myself. But Sheik was very nice. I felt he was almost like a member of the family. He said that's all right. So my uncle told him, you know, I didn't know too many names but I would make out. So he said that's all right. And she was a trio. We went to Burris and we played and that's about the dirty job I played.
And you could play by ear though?

Yeah. Well you see my uncle would hum the thing and he'd say well this goes like this and he'd play and I'd learn it like that. But I also was running the popular tunes of the day, with stop arrangements. What song was popular then? I'll tell you one song that was very popular, I'll never forget, was Long Ago and Far Away. My uncle still has that music now. What's it about? Long Ago and Far Away, the hit parade, number one on the hit parade. It was, I mean it's not no jazz numbers. It's somebody like Judy Gollum sang that. I don't know who. But it was Long Ago and Far Away, there was If I Love You.
And so.

So you know when that just do the. Well we wouldn't do this on these jobs. When my uncle would get a job, and sometimes he was lucky enough to get a job where I could use the whole family. Say nine men. He'd use my cousin Charles, myself and him. Three saxophones and my two cousins played trumpet. And he'd get a trombone player. I believe Homer Eugene would play trombone. And he liked brother groups. I noticed that because he'd get Mac Lane and his son to play banjo and bass. And he'd get the Eugene brothers to play trombone if he could, if they weren't working. And I can't remember who he would use on drums because they were all older and I was not. I didn't get to know the rhythm section, but a complete rhythm section. And then Michael Climes would play piano at times. And then too there was always music at Malcolm in his house, you see. Sometimes the whole family would come over and there'd be two bass players, two bass players. Michael Climes would play piano. He'd play drums and then Charles went to play on the saxophone. And we'd play together and he'd say, well hit this, I'll tell you. He'd play a drum, but he still plays a little now. And he'd say play this, play such and such a note. Because once Jay McShane came over there. Jay McShane?
Yeah.

My uncle was working, my Uncle Presley was working with Jay McShane's band. He came to the house, which was right across from where my Uncle Oxlade's done. One corner, another uptown, downtown. And Jay McShane, which is known as a blues pianist, and he was singing the blues, and he'd give us each a note to hit it and direct us as to when to hit it.
Yeah, all this was in the 40s.

Probably it was 46, something right? 46 or 45. I don't believe it was 47 because I graduated from high school in 47 with this band, Joe Jones, this big band, we played for the prom. And that 46 dollars, it was six dollars then, put me in the union. So I've been in the union long enough to be a lifetime member, but I'm not old enough. And I was joining the union when I was 16. See, which is all, next year it'll be 30 years. But I believe you have to be 65. See, and I'm 45, so I have 20 more years. And I've been in the union almost 30 years. Did you go old now? Yeah, but I'm not in there long enough. I mean, I'm not old enough. I'm in there long enough because there are guys that haven't been in there as long as me, but they're old enough, you see.
So who was in Joe Jones' band at first?
Oh, the first band is the guy that said Melvin Lasty, Wilbur Hogan played trumpet, Wilbur Hogan played drums, he's dead now. He's got a brother that's a very good pianist.
I know, yeah.

Edmund Hogan, that's his brother. And Warren Skinner, he's a, I don't have a picture of that band here. I had a picture, I don't know what happened to it. Warren Skinner's a physical ed teacher, he played baritone sax. And Lloyd Bellamy, he's a musician around town, I believe he stopped playing, he played saxophone. He lived right next to the rhythm club. He was in the rhythm club, or Jackson. He was in Jackson. His family owned that house, they're still on it, if I'm not mistaken. And we had, in the trombones we had Tommy Shelvin who went to California, he's a bass player with Roy Brown, played bass now.
Did he play with Tommy originally? Probably did, yeah.

Yeah, he started out, he played bass, yeah. And then he left and went to California, Tommy Shelvin. All of us were in the Spoketee Washington High School band. And Rupert Robinson played, he's a cab driver right now. And you catch him every day right now on, by Wolverine, on Canal and Rapport. He's got a V8 cab, all the cabs are black, colored painted black. Rupert Rob plays guitar, he was our guitar player. Still plays? Yeah, he plays when he gets his job, but it's more or less a second, not a main way to make a dollar. But he still plays, he plays every now and then. He played guitar and we used, Joe Jones played piano. But Joe Jones was more or less a piano player, I think, that had to have music to play. Because one night he forgot the music and he didn't play at all and nobody knew it. Because we had a big band, you see. But I'll tell you what he is, he's energetic guy.
He had a big arrangement right in front of him.

Yeah, we had an energetic guy and he's a good hustler and he's a good talker, if you know him. And he can, he's good at finding work. Oh, yeah. So he talked, he talked the president into using the band, if he could get to, if he listened to it. But at this time he was just coming into this and the bands, well the band we had wasn't well known. And we wasn't, we waked up to, we played, we played Autocrat Club, a dance, we played Booker T. Washington Prown, and we played prongs for different schools. The band lasted about, I'd say, to 49 when they broke up. Because Hogan went in the Army and a couple of the other guys went in the service. And I found that I could do better playing with a smaller band, I could make a few dollars more, because we might work once a month at the most. And I was out of school and I was trying to help with the expenses in the house, because we, it was five of us, you see. But I'm the only one that played, my father was sick. And my uncle would get maybe two jobs for me a week, so I just had to leave the band, I see. And I would get into where I could play a little better. And we'd play, I'd play with, I'd play with a guy like Sheep when they have something, and the Handy Brothers, they would get something, I'd play with them. So you were playing both Dixieland and- Well yeah, if you would call it that. But at the time, I just, yeah we just played, well Sheep played the same way he played, but they weren't, they weren't labeled as they do now, just would play it. It wasn't saying he's playing Dixieland.
I would just have called it music. Music, yeah.

But they would play the tunes at the time, because it was, once it hadn't been too long that people were playing those tunes as everyday music. But now it's like Dixieland or Rock or something, but they didn't have all that. And Sheep, we played, like Caldonia was a blues out then, the closest thing to rhythm and blues. We played Caldonia. Yeah. And we might have played, at the time I didn't know Musgraat and Rambo, but we played tunes of that order. Musgraat and Rambo, like played the Sheik of Araby, and we played Lady Be Good, everybody played Lady Be Good at the time. And Can't Escape from You, that's another tune they played. And we played tunes like that, and they played Caldonia, or whatever was out on the the jukebox, like Caldonia was a- You played like the, you know, one of the jukebox hits were out on the- Yeah, but that was also with the same band. That's right. So you couldn't say it was a Dixieland band. Do you speak French? No. Not at all. Neither does my mother. And we would play and finally I got so that things got kinda bad. I wasn't. The most we could make around here was eight dollars, ten dollars a night, and I got married.
Did you have a, when you were playing, you said you only played a couple times a month,

did you have a day journal? Yeah. Oh yeah. First I worked at the charity hospital where my mother just retired from. I was an orderly, an award, and I worked in every phase I believe of the hospital. I was in an accident room a while. I was in an admitting room. Oh wow. I worked, which my mother's a retired nurse and my sister's a nurse, and sort of runs in a family. So, that, this family, I mean, it wasn't too hard to get a job around that being, and so I worked there until the hospital paid so low, such a low pay when I got, I had a couple of kids, and I was making, I've been making twenty dollars a week in 1951. Wow. And it would come to forty dollars every two weeks, and that, that, you know, things weren't
that high, but it still wasn't no money. Okay, why don't we, we can stop it.
But it's gonna, it's gonna run off, it, run it to the, uh. You wanna run it all the way to the end? Yeah, to the very end, you know, it works fine. I just have to get a new reel. And, uh, I...
I played 48 when I first went there.
See I came here in 49.
49, but I used to go there, it was around 48, but that was the only place you could get those records. Padres and Barone.
Yeah it was 439 Barone, Norwich records here.
Barone and Padres, that's right.
Yeah.
Yeah well that's where I used to get these, that was the only place they had dial records. And they had boots at the time, you could go, they don't have that now.
Boots, you could play your records.
Yeah you could see if you liked it.
See what you liked it.
Yeah that's right.
I believe 78 was 75 cents at the time.
Something like that.
Yeah they weren't, albums weren't even, had it even got to be then.
No LPs.
Yeah but all 78's. Not in the late 40s.

All 78's, I don't remember seeing it. If there was, I believe, Jazz to Philharmonic was the first LP I saw. And that's where I first heard Charlie Park on him. He played Lady Be Good and I said yeah that's the saxophone play I wanted. Well I really first heard him when I was graduating from high school, because Wallace, Wallace Allen was in my class, he and I graduated together. Was he in the band? No. Wallace was, well he was a man when I was a kid because he had been in the Navy band. Oh yeah. And the band was sort of like a step down for him. He was playing, he had his own band at the Dewdrop at the time. But after I left with Joe Jones, Joe Jones was graduating from high school, the next band step for me was Wallace. We went back to school again and we took up Short Hand, Typing and Geek. This was in 48, I remember this very well. And Wallace was in the class and Wallace was playing with Harold DeJong at the Opera House. Opera House. Uh huh. And we had been, he said, he told me, he said Harold needed someone to play in his place. And he said, well, do you think he could make it? I said, I don't know. So he said, come out and try. So I went and played with him that night. And of course I had been listening to these Charlie Parker records that I had bought from this shop. And they were playing, one or two of them they played with Salt Peanuts at the time, getting into the bebop thing. And Harold said, I'll never forget, he said, that must be a CG Conn you're playing on, because that's what he still talks about. And I said, yeah, that's what it is. And we played and he said, the next night he took off and I played and I made ten dollars, which was very good for that time. Because I used to give my mother half of what I made and I'd keep half and I still had good money. I made five dollars, but it would last me a week. See. And so I played, Wallace got a little band together and we called it the Bebop, that's in this book here. Oh yeah, the Bebop. The Bebop Jockers, yeah, I remember. The Bebop Jockers, we never made a dime. I believe the best thing we had, we worked Bourbon Street for three weeks. And that band made, I believe it made 60 dollars a week, which was good, I believe it was 1949, it was before I got married in 1949. We made 60 dollars a week for three weeks. And that was very, very good money. And we played the band a while and I believe Wallace, we couldn't find out what we couldn't find any work. And the next band, one of them was the Johnson Brothers, they called me. Johnson Brothers. Yeah, Johnson Brothers. And this was 49 also, the end of 49. And I worked with them. They had a band that was very popular. They played dances. They played six nights a week, different places. Plas Johnson is right now in Hollywood, he plays tenor. He's the brother who's the most famous. He's most famous for the Pink Panther. You ever hear that? The comedy, the saxophone solo, that's Plas. That's him. He was playing like that then, the same way. He played tenor. I was playing alto sax and they had a five piece band and they wanted an alto sax, because they were going to make a record. And I think that's the first record I made called Mellow Mama. What's that? We made it at Booker T. Washington, Booker T. Washington Auditorium. They brought these things, you like this. Yeah. And Paul Gaten supervised it. Oh, for what? I couldn't tell you. Oh wait, yes I can too. Deluxe.
Deluxe.
Deluxe. I believe Deluxe had another company that they- Regal, was that?
Well, it was Deluxe. I tell you. Yeah, because, well that was the company.

Deluxe it was, forty-nine. We'll look it up. Yeah, Mellow Mama, that's the name of it. What was it released as? It was released as Mellow Mama. The Johnson Brothers? The Johnson Brothers. The Johnson Brothers. The Johnson Brothers. That's right, Mellow Mama. I believe it was a, because it took us a year to get the money, and at the time it was forty dollars for a recording session, which was still a lot of money. And forty-nine was plenty of money. And, because I played with that band, and that's the best band I ever worked with till the day I think. It is. I know it. It is. Claes Johnson, his sister Gwen sang, Raymond played piano, Lloyd Lambert played bass, same Lloyd who's up there now with me, with Thomas Jefferson. Lloyd Lambert played bass, Edward Blackwell played drums, who went with Arnett Coleman. And Raymond played piano. And Raymond played piano. And Raymond played piano. And Ray Charles played trumpet. He went with Ray Charles later on. He's in New York now. I believe he wrote a couple of tunes for Ray Charles. And then later on, Harold Batiste, who had specialty records here, was the representative, he came in and he played baritone. He came in and played baritone I'd say about 1950, or 51, because he was going to Dillard then, which was a very good clarinet player. And he came in a band and he played baritone. And he's, right now, in fact he's the one that discovered Sonny and Cher. He discovered Sonny, which led to Cher. But he doesn't get any credit for it. We produced all of us early. Well the last time Cher and Sonny came in, he was conducting for them. It was the year I had the accident, because I was on credit the last time I saw them. Nineteen seventy-seven, there with the Fairmount. Sonny and Cher, he was conducting for Sonny and Cher. He discovered Sonny here.
Yeah, well I think Sonny was working for Specialty at the same time. Yeah.

But he's the one that discovered Sonny. He brought him with Specialty. He produced the first record. He found Sonny here? That's what I read. But I know he discovered, he put them together. He put Sonny, he started, made Sonny's first record. Now how Cher got in there, I don't know, but he produced all of their records until they got on a big scale. And he was conducting for them, whenever they were going. He conducted for them all over.
I heard that he was the brains behind.

He's one of the smartest, well one of the best musicians I know. Aside from financial things, I mean he's a national down-to-date musician. Because we were in a little Army Reserve band he was in also, where I learned a lot. This guy was a professor at Dillon and he had the band in charge and we'd go to camp twice a year, once a year, and we'd go to meetings twice a week. And he would show us things that he was teaching in college. And Harold Batiste was one of his students. And I saw Harold sit down and write like you're writing now, and write five tunes just like that. And that was in the fifties. That's how good he is. He's better today. He was playing piano and he formed this company, EFO, later on. Yeah I remember that. He started that out. And then he went to California and he's up there now, he's going to Hollywood right now. But anyway, the Johnson Brothers, what broke that band was the Korean War, because players went to the service. And when he went to, this was about 51 or 52. He went to the service during the time of the Korean conflict, I'll say, and that broke the band up. And so when he went to the service, I went to Detroit. Yeah, that's the last band up there. I went to Detroit and my Uncle Percy, I stayed with him and I started working up there with him for a while. But I couldn't get situated right. And I would make like, I would work two months at the Ford plant and I was working two nights a week with him. But they laid me off and never called me back. So the music work wasn't enough to make a living off.
Were the bands different up in Detroit?

At the time, yes, very definitely. They played, they were leaning toward a more, I'd say, a rock swing type, show type band. See, at the time it was like Illinois Jacket, tenor players, played like that. And I was playing alto. I was trying to play alto like Charlie Parker. So the thing up there was a show like tenor, piano and drums, playing for a stage show. And a honking type tenor player, which I hadn't got into yet. So as a rule, the guys that were up there already doing it, I had to take a back seat to it because I wasn't good enough. And I didn't have time to sit around and get into it, so I came back home. But when I came back home, that looked like it was the right thing to do. Because I started working, I was working with Dave Bartholomew also. And I started making recordings with him.
Yeah, was that, when did you first start working with Dave Bartholomew?

First, I believe this was around, oh it was a little after 1950, it was before I went to Detroit. But after I left the Johnson Brothers, I went with Dave for a while, and when he worked at the Pelican on Rapport Street, he opened it up. And he was a very good trumpet player. At the time he was playing music. He had arraignments on everything. And he was a very good reader. He was making it strictly off his band and he worked six nights a week on his Johnson. Yeah, he had to do a hot band. And his band had good guys. He had Earl Palmer, who was one of the best drummers around now in Hollywood, was playing drums with him. And he had Mac Lane, or it was Mac Lane, playing guitar. And Salvador, who was playing piano, who left, he went in the Army. Very good pianist. And he had Red Tyler, myself, he had Clarence Hall, Myer Kennedy, or Boater, who did. He had originally six pieces and later, well Myer took sick and so I joined the band at Myer's place. Then Red Tyler was in the band. Red Tyler was there before me. Probably. He was there from the beginning. Yeah, and that band. And there was another before. Who's playing bass? Oh, with Frank Fields, one of the best bass players in the round right now. He's playing with Papa French now. Very good, very nice guy. He's a musician. Yeah, he fixes television, things like that. Now he might, maybe he can fix these. I don't know.
He's got in mind television.

I'll see it. He fixes television, yeah. He's got in mind. There was another band I played before, before I forgot about, was Clyde Carr was teaching. Oh, you played with Clyde Carr? He was teaching at very good trumpet player. His father, the one that, now I say it's a senior, there's two Clyde, but one's a junior. Yeah, Clyde junior. Well, Clyde was teaching at Booker T for a year before I left there. He was into syncopation, Jimmy Luntz and things. And he had a little band, a rehearsal band, we played concerts free, we didn't make any money out of it. And Tyler was in that band also.
Yeah, he played with Curb.

Yeah, we had, we must have had, well I said 30 some pieces. And out of the whole band, there's about five of us that still play. But Wardell Cazare is one. Yeah, Wardell Cazare. He played trumpet. Delton Russo, he's still playing. That's the guys that I remember out of the band that got to be something later on. Tyler and myself, that's all. But Clyde Carr was a, he was a musician's musician. Everything we played with him was written. Everything. He didn't play anything that wasn't written out. He never played anything that was blues or Dixieland or anything like that. Everything was like, he had an arraignment on Rhapsody in Blue, in a swing version. That's to give you an idea. But strictly I learned a lot about reading under him. In fact, he's one of the best reading teachers I've ever had. And the things he, the way he's teaching now, then if you find someone to teach like that now, it would really be good. Because the teachers don't teach like that now, like he was teaching. He's a, I believe he's teaching mathematics. He's not even teaching music now in a school. He's a very, very good musician and a good trumpet player. He was with Lyra when my uncle was with him. But I went to Detroit and came back and that's when I got back with them. Got into the blues thing that's in his book with Smiley Lewis. I worked with Smiley Lewis. Made a record, a few records, The Bells Are Ringing, Blue Monday, things like that. Imperial. Because Dave had Imperial and everything he could put me on. He put me on. And I worked at it. So you got in with Dave's band. Yeah. Doing gigs. In 52.
On the bandstand. Did he put you in the studio?

Yeah. He put me in the studio. Yeah. No, well, the way he would, he would switch it around. How would he work? If it was something that he could use me on, he would. But the first records he made, I believe, was, for Imperial, was The Fat Man with Fats Time. You were Fats. Yeah, I wasn't with Fats then. And later on, the guy got sick and the guy that took sick, I replaced him, so I replaced him in the studio. He used Joe Harris sometimes. Sometimes it would be three of us, three reeds. Sometimes. And then I got a baritone, because once his band had built up to five reeds. Three altos. Warren Bell, the guy who was on the news, his father, plays alto. Very good. One of the best around him. He's a modern jazz alto player and he won't play anything else. Warren Bell. He's working on the same. He has a good job. But anyway, Warren Bell was playing alto, lead alto. And I was playing lead alto. And then Maya was playing third alto. So I said, well, I borrowed a baritone. That's how I got into playing baritone. And played baritone, so we had a full reed section. And so whenever he'd get a recording section, he'd try it on a baritone. So I made a, I believe I made a first record on baritone as well, going down the line. Because I don't think there was anybody making them before that. I might be wrong, but I think I'm one of the first to make a baritone on a rhythm and blues record in New Orleans. Down the line with Fat Man Matthews, Imperial record it was. Oh, yeah. And then after Tyler started making. Was that your first session with Dave? No, the first one I made, I played alto. I live my life to please myself. Wait, I'm going to have to guess on that. Yeah, that's with Dave Witholomew. With Dave. Imperial. Tommy Ridgely, Dave Witholomew. I don't know whose name it's under, but it was Tommy Ridgely. It was under Tommy Ridgely. Was Tommy Sidney? Yeah, Tommy Sidney.
Well, the problem was under Tommy Sidney.

Tommy Ridgely, Dave Witholomew, Earl Palmer. It was a trio of voices. I live my life to please myself, don't worry about nobody else. That's the very first record I made for Imperial. Have you ever seen the first record I made? No, no, the first record I made was Mellow Mama I said. Yeah, well yeah. But I didn't record it no more for a good while and then I made that one. But Mellow Mama was strictly a written thing for this guy to sing with the Johnson Brothers. But this must be the first one. This is the first one I made for Imperial. How much did y'all get for a session? Forty-one dollars and twenty-five cents.
For a session.

For a three-hour session, four sides. If you could cut four sides in one hour, that was it. Now if you had to cut four more sides, there was another session. But it was forty-one dollars and twenty-five cents. And I made, at the time, I made three recording sessions in one day. I've seen it with Smiley Lewis. And we had done just that many. I mean that's how big recording was at the time.
And you'd stay in the studio? Yeah.
We wouldn't stay there that long. We could make a session in an hour if we, the guys had gotten so new.
Well I knew it was all live, you know, and you'd cut it as you went. Yeah. So you mean Dave would cut as many things as he could? Sometimes.

He said we'd want to get two sessions out in a day. So if Smiley Lewis would have enough tunes for two sessions, we'd do them. And sometimes we'd do one take and he'd say, I know I can't do it no better than that. And he'd say, what do y'all think? He'd say, no we can't do it any better than that. So that's a take. Now a record at the time I believe would last three minutes. So you'd play three minutes and that's a take. Well suppose you did four tunes in three minutes, twelve minutes, well counting the time it takes to play back. I'd say a half hour you could do a session, you know, with everything right. But I'd give it an hour at the most. We could do a session. And then sometime we'd do another. We could do a next session, take a break for a half hour because that same Buster used to be next door to the studio. Some of that's in that book there. Buster was on Dumaine and Rampart, St. Claude. And we'd, at the time, red beans, rice, hot sauce was 35 cents and a Coke was a dime. And for 50 cents you could get more than you want to eat. And we'd make a session, go by Buster's and 50 cents, and eat like I don't know what and come back and make another one.
How would you do a couple of sessions every week?

Well sometimes, you know, it would run sometimes. We'd do a session, like I said, I'd do three in one day, then I might not do none for maybe a month. Then I'd do one, then maybe one. I did, I made quite a few, but I wasn't the number one man in the sessions. Red Tyler, Lee Allen, which in that book, they were number, like I was about number two. Nat Peril, I made a lot. And then Toussaint Allen, Toussaint started using me on some, which I got into on some of the things he did.
So what other, besides Dave and Tommy, you said you were behind Fat Man Matthews?

Yeah, Tommy Ridgely, Pee Wee Creighton. Oh, you did the Pee Wee Creighton? One of them for Imperial. That was supposed to be a very important session. T-Bone Walker. I remember one tune I had a solo, and I'd like to hear it now, you better go now, yours too. For T-Bone? No, it was Pee Wee Creighton. Pee Wee Creighton, yeah. And T-Bone Walker's session was, I believe, written. But see, we'd do stuff, people would come in town today, and they'd say, well, let's get with Dave, and about two days later, we'd do a second, we wouldn't see him anymore. I also did the voice record that Sherilyn Lee made, I'm Gone. I'm Gone.
Yeah.

Uh-huh. There were little kids out of school, that's in there. They're only like fourteen. I did their, right, they were going to Clark. I did their first session, and I didn't know what they were going to do. But most of their stuff was similar. And a lot of that stuff got on the piano, I played baritone though. Leonard Lee, that's his name, he's still in New Orleans. He got on the piano and he played what he wanted and we put a little background to it. Most of those had arrangements? Yes, all of them were head arrangements. In those times.
Well how would Dave conduct a set?

He would say, I want this. Now if he had to sketch something out, he would, later on I believe he would sketch out a line. Me playing a baritone, I'd transpose, but a guy playing a piano would play the same thing. And that's how we did most of them, we'd write a line. Now later on, when I, with Fats, he was like one session was all music, that was Frank wrote. But during that time it was all head stuff. He said, Fats would start playing, or whoever it was, would start playing and he'd try a riff and say, what do you think about this? Make a riff. And if the riff fit, or if he had a specific riff, he said, well come on, make this behind me and I'd make that.
Did you find Fats had a lot of creativity or would he rely on Dave a lot?

Well I think it would be what, half and half. I couldn't say one was any better than another. I think they were good for each other. Because he would have stuff and Dave would have stuff. See, like for instance, I made Blue Monday with Smiley Lewis first. And then later on they gave it to Fats and put a baritone solo in it. And Fats hit what's bigger than Smiley Lewis. See so it was Smiley and Dave's tune first. Then Fats got it later on. Well everybody associates it with Fats. It's like I'm going to be a wheel someday, I made that with Bobby Over the River. Yeah, Bobby Over the River. Yeah. Okay, and then later on Fats got it. See so one thing was good for the other one. See one was good for the other. So I left, I left, I didn't get close, I wasn't even thinking about Garmin Fats then. Because I had a, when I came back I had a Dave job, a pretty good job. Make 40 dollars a week, which was real good money then. And I was working with Joe Jones again. He had Joe Jones when he started this little small record company. I mean a small band. And Capitol Records came here and we made a record for them. And at the time it was under the hood up there, New Orleans Band that made a record for Capitol. And I can't tell you what the name of that was. I can't remember, Joe Jones made a record for Capitol. Must have been 53, something like, 53 or 54.
I remember that but I can't remember.

Yeah, because Dave, I believe the guy's name was Dave Cavanaugh, Dave or something. Yeah, he was a tenor, alto player. Yeah, right. He came down, he didn't play though, he just came and directed. Yeah. Well, produced it in our session. We made it at the same Cosmo Studios. Right. Cosmo hadn't moved yet from off, off, off, off, off, off. And Joe Jones was working at this place where I was working. We were loading, Stevens Band, Paper Company. We were loading trucks up all day with supplies like toilet paper, paper to wrap stuff up in. And we'd work sometimes till five in the evening. And leave there and Joe would get a job for five pieces. And at the same time Dick Van Dyke was here. And we did his show, we did his show, several times. We played on his show at least three times, I'd say, Dick Van Dyke's show. We didn't get anything for it. It was advertisement at the time. And television was new. It was the only channel. Yeah, six. So if anybody had television, they saw it because that was all it was on. It came on around four in the evening. Dick Van Dyke's show. And because when I heard Dick Van Dyke was going nationwide, I was surprised. We used to be on his show, he used to always have a different, come out with a different thing. He would be sort of like a Milton Berle thing. Yeah, he was sort of a comedian. He was trying to a lot. Yeah. He put on all kinds of crazy outfits. I think he experimented a lot when he was here. Yeah, he was trying to find himself. And we would play, and they had a band, they had another band too that would play. And we'd play out one or two numbers. We'd always play something that way. We were doing a rhythm and blues thing at that time. Because we were always doing something that was current, something that was like a shake, rattle and roll or something like that. We did those kind of things. And I did so much as a front to the band until people thought I was Joe Jones. See we all had tenor and rhythm. I was playing tenor and Joe playing piano. And we had several drummers. Justin played with us at that time. Justin and Plot Seed. But they were both, and Prevost was the bass player. The same Prevost was at the Preservation Hall.
Yeah.

Yeah, because we got in an incident late on over the river there where we all had to leave. Prevost's bass got broke up. And right, that was before I ever thought about leaving. But Joe had a disagreement with one of the guys in the band and he fired him. I said, well if you fired him I'm going to leave too. Dalton. And when he left we went with Guitar Slam then. That was in 54. Who was it? That's how I went with Guitar Slam. Joe Jones. Who was the other guy? Dalton Russo, a trumpet player. Yeah. He played with Tiger. He was with Tiger. That's how we were together. We were like brothers. Dalton Russo? Yeah. We all played together the same. We were roommates. So we both left. Get to our Slam he needed, it's a funny thing, he needed a saxophone player and a trumpet player at the same time. So Jose called him. Jose Hill? Yeah.
He was the manager.
Jose called him and said he needed a saxophone player. So he told me about it because I wasn't working at all. And Joe just thought we wouldn't work anywhere.
So I said, he said, I'm taking it.

I said, well I've never been on the road, I'll take it too because I'm not doing it. And Guitar Slam was working at the time. We were getting twenty dollars a night, seven nights a week. And we could get a room for two dollars a night. We could get a meal in cities like New York for a dollar, less than a dollar.
So you went?

That was my 46-year-old song. Who else was in the band with Slam? With Slam, when I got there it was Lloyd Lambert was the manager, leader of the band. Slam was featured at Traction, he was going to Slam's band, but Lloyd Lambert was really the leader, bass player. And Cotton, Lawrence Cotton was playing piano. And Lloyd played bass, Oscar played drums. Oscar Moore. Yeah. He was with Slam before any of them. And Joe Tillman played tenor sax. Gus played alto, Gus Fontenet. And I played baritone. I was in the band, it's a baritone player. I didn't have a baritone. And I had a good friend, Ellis Marcellus, he's still a good friend, and a wonderful musician, the greatest piano player I'll ever know. He was playing baritone sax. He would be playing with us with Joe Jones sometimes. So he lost. I said, in some kind of way he said, I'll lend you the baritone, because I don't want it no more. He stopped playing baritone, I'm about to play the piano. And I was supposed to buy it from him, but he finally gave it to me. And he loaned me a baritone, and I went to play baritone for about two years, so in 56. And I came on Cry to State. We played Apollo Theater. At the time when Apollo Theater, if you couldn't play, you had to play for a show, they'd put another man in there, you wouldn't make a dime. You had to be able to play the theater, to read the show, and you never saw it before. See, they'd come up there with the show, like they do at the film. No, they were doing it. If you couldn't play that show, somebody would come there and take your spot. So, well. How long were you in the road to the slip? About two years. A little bit better. I was all of 56. And all of 55. Now I don't know if I went there in 55 or late 54. Because they, no, it had to be 55, because they had a 55 wagon, 55 Ford wagon. That's how you all would get around? That's right, a wagon. I met them in Macon, Georgia and went on a train. And they had a 55 Ford wagon, and as many as nine of us went on that wagon at times.
Did it have some like, like, sling his name on the side? Guitar, Slim and his orchestra. And his orchestra.

Now he traveled in a Cadillac at the time. When y'all would travel in a? In a Ford 55 station wagon. And he had a Cadillac. He had a Cadillac. That would be just like Slim. Well, that's like all those singers at that time. That was the thing. The Cadillac comes in. See, the Cadillac would ride in town facing the band behind. See, that was, make a grand entrance and everybody would come around and they'd see the band and then they'd go to the, we'd always get in town before dark. See the band and they'd come to the dance. But he was, his popularity, he was good, but nobody really knew how good he was. See, Ray Charles got his thing from listening to guitar, Slim. And I never read anywhere where Ray Charles wrote that down. He got his thing because Ray Charles at the time was trying to get started around here. And his band, in fact Slim's band made Ray Charles' voice record, the Ezra Ray Charles, Don't You Know Baby. I wasn't in the band. They used another baritone player.
But the band didn't have a baritone. I heard a lot of descriptions about Slim's personality.

Well Slim, he was not intelligent. He was sort of like a person that would come up on the phone. But he wasn't. The most harm, the most harm he did was himself. He drank a lot. I believe that's what killed him. He drank heavily. And he was, a lot of people made money off him because he didn't have the right manager. I mean everybody was trying to see how much they could get out of it. But I think Hosey was the best manager he had because Hosey put a band with him and sort of handled his affairs. It was wild enough that Hosey had to bear him because he stood at Tivito most of the time. But he was all right, fella. And he would come to me and he said, I'll never be the musician, you all. And he said, I respect musicians. But he said that he was not no great musician. He never thought he was great like some of the guys. He said he just was a plain, ordinary guitar picker. He used to pick cotton and his fingers were very long. I guess that's what he fingered the guitar. And something he did, I've never seen too many guys. He'd walk all around with a guitar.
Yeah, he used to.

He'd hang down from the top of the roof with his guitar and play at the same time. He made a good attraction. He was a good visual attraction. That was most of his popularity. Yeah. But he had some tunes that he sang if you listen to them. His last thing that he recorded was, If I Had My Life To Live Over. Now he died right after that. He looked into that. And another thing he did, Suffering Mind. Now that was close to Ray Charles as Ray Charles. Ray Charles heard that and got his thing from that. But Suffering Mind, I haven't heard it, but it sounds more like Ray Charles. Right now it would sound like that. It would sound like a crude Ray Charles. Because the band was playing the same type of style. Slim wasn't very sophisticated. No, he was playing, he'd come out with a red suit on, a green suit on. But he had a million selling record and the country people liked him. That's why we did our best in Florida, Mississippi, Alabama.
How did you rule? We broke records.

We broke records in Florida. Poems and Howlandale had more people there over a two week period than anybody else broke records. And he, see the people, he would come on later, we would play and he'd come on later and take off. And then we'd take intermission and then we'd play again and he'd come on. It was like a show. Yeah. Like a traveling show. Yeah, we did the warm up. Yeah. And the band was, another thing, we had a lot of good arrangements. So Lloyd did arrangement? No. No. No. No. No. No.
We got the third reel on.
I wanted to ask you about it. I'm up to with guitar slim.
I wanted to ask you about people like guitar slim and fast domino. How many keys were those two playing?

Well, now, guitar slim, I'll take it from him. He played what you call a choke guitar. He had a selector, a key selector. He played in actually one key. But he had a key selector. I see a lot of these rock players now. You slide it up and down. A capo, it's called a capo, but we call it a choke. And he would put it to a certain place, and where he would put it would be F or E flat. Now he sang in different keys, but he actually played in one. I mean it sounded like a paradox. Whereas he's playing the same way but the selector's changing it. In an open position. Which I play a little guitar myself. So I know what that is. He's playing in an open position. In other words, he could take the guitar and strum it. It's like a playing way, he would hit an E chord with one string down, held down. And if he'd slide it up to E flat, and the F, the top fret would be F. Like that F sharp to second one, G to third, you see? Yeah. And that way he would be playing the same fingers, but it would be in a different key. He didn't retune his guitar album.
No.

No, he played it in one way. I know who did. I played with John Lee Hooker, and he did. He would retune. John Lee Hooker? Yes. I played with. I played with. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

Yeah, alright.

segments.title: Reel opening, names and date
segments.summary: Allen and Jones set up the first reel, Ford gives his full name, and the date is 10 December 1975.

segments.title: Birth, musical family, uncle teaching him clarinet, first Mardi Gras job
segments.summary: Ford was born in Charity Hospital in 1929; his uncles and cousins were musicians. His uncle started him on clarinet around 1944, he played a Mardi Gras parade with the Eureka band for 15 dollars, then a job with the Adams family group across the river.

segments.title: Working across the river in Algiers and Gretna
segments.summary: Ford describes taking the ferry and bus to jobs in Algiers, Gretna and Marrero, where there was more work, and the Moulin Rouge.

segments.title: Clubs across the river and getting his own clarinet
segments.summary: After a phone interruption, Ford names the Moulin Rouge, Specs and the Moonlight Inn, and tells how his uncle repaired an old Albert-system clarinet that became his first instrument.

segments.title: Albert system versus Boehm system clarinet
segments.summary: Ford explains the fingering and tone differences between the Albert and Boehm clarinet systems and which players use each.

segments.title: Why he moved from clarinet to saxophone
segments.summary: Ford says the music of the time called for saxophone, Dixieland players could not make a living, and clarinet is a good foundation. His mother signed for his first alto.

segments.title: Big swing bands he heard as a teenager
segments.summary: Ford describes Herbert Leary's swing band, which his uncle played in, and why it made him want to learn to read music.

segments.title: Booker T. Washington school band and Joe Jones's big band
segments.summary: Ford and Melvin Lastie formed a swing band from the Booker T. Washington band, rehearsing at Corpus Christi. He also met Kid Sheik and played an early job with him.

segments.title: Learning tunes by ear and popular songs of the day
segments.summary: Ford's uncle hummed and played tunes for him, and he learned hit-parade songs and stop arrangements.

segments.title: Uncle's family bands and a visit from Jay McShann
segments.summary: Ford's uncle used the whole family on jobs, with other musician families, and music was constant at home. Jay McShann once came to the house and gave them notes to play.

segments.title: Graduating in 1947 and joining the musicians' union
segments.summary: Ford graduated in 1947 after playing the prom with the Joe Jones big band, and joined the union at 16.

segments.title: Members of the Joe Jones high-school big band
segments.summary: Ford names the band's members, mostly Booker T. Washington students, and what became of them.

segments.title: End of the school band and smaller jobs with Kid Sheik
segments.summary: The big band broke up around 1949; Ford turned to smaller groups with Sheik and the Handy Brothers, playing popular tunes that were not yet labelled Dixieland.

segments.title: Marriage and his day job as a hospital orderly
segments.summary: Pay from music was too low, so Ford married and worked at Charity Hospital, earning 20 dollars a week in 1951.

segments.title: Tape pause and reel change
segments.summary: The interviewers decide to stop the tape and change reels.

segments.title: Record shop on Barone Street and buying 78s
segments.summary: Ford and Allen recall the record shop where you could audition 78 rpm discs in booths in the late 1940s.

segments.title: Hearing Charlie Parker, Wallace Allen, the Bebop Jockers and the Johnson Brothers
segments.summary: Ford first heard Parker on Jazz at the Philharmonic, sat in for Harold Dejan at the Opera House, played in Wallace Allen's Bebop Jockers, then joined the Johnson Brothers and made 'Mellow Mama' for Deluxe.

segments.title: Johnson Brothers personnel and Harold Battiste
segments.summary: Ford calls this the best band he worked with, lists its members and describes Harold Battiste, who joined on baritone and later worked with Sonny and Cher.

segments.title: Battiste as musician, the Korean War breakup and going to Detroit
segments.summary: Ford praises Battiste, then explains the Korean War ended the Johnson Brothers and he went to Detroit to stay with his Uncle Percy, where music work was not enough.

segments.title: Detroit bands compared with New Orleans
segments.summary: Detroit bands favoured show-style honking tenor, so Ford as a Parker-style alto player took a back seat and returned home.

segments.title: Joining Dave Bartholomew's band at the Pelican
segments.summary: Ford recalls Bartholomew as a trumpeter and reader with a strong six-night band including Earl Palmer, Red Tyler and Frank Fields.

segments.title: Clyde Kerr's rehearsal band and returning to Bartholomew and Smiley Lewis
segments.summary: Ford describes studying reading with Clyde Kerr and his written-out band, then rejoining Bartholomew and recording with Smiley Lewis for Imperial.

segments.title: First Imperial recordings and early baritone
segments.summary: Ford explains how he got into the studio, took up baritone and made 'I Live My Life to Please Myself' with Tommy Ridgley as his first Imperial record.

segments.title: Session pay and the pace of recording
segments.summary: Sessions paid 41.25 dollars for three hours and four sides, with several sessions in a day, and the band ate at Buster Holmes's between them.

segments.title: How often he recorded and who else was called
segments.summary: Ford did sessions in bursts, ranking behind Red Tyler and Lee Allen, and also worked for Allen Toussaint.

segments.title: Sessions behind Pee Wee Crayton, T-Bone Walker and Shirley and Lee
segments.summary: Ford recalls Imperial sessions with Tommy Ridgley, Pee Wee Crayton and T-Bone Walker, and Shirley and Lee's first record.

segments.title: Head arrangements, Fats Domino and Bartholomew's collaboration
segments.summary: Ford explains how Bartholomew built records from head riffs, how the two split creativity with Fats, and how 'Blue Monday' went from Smiley Lewis to Fats.

segments.title: Joe Jones's Capitol record and the Dick Van Dyke show
segments.summary: Ford worked with Joe Jones's small band, cut a Capitol record at Cosimo's, played on the Dick Van Dyke TV show and worked a day job loading trucks.

segments.chapter: On the road with Guitar Slim
segments.title: Leaving Joe Jones to join Guitar Slim
segments.summary: After Joe Jones fired a bandmate, Ford and Dalton Russo left, and Guitar Slim's manager hired them for 20 dollars a night.

segments.chapter: On the road with Guitar Slim
segments.title: Slim's band members and playing baritone at the Apollo
segments.summary: Ford lists the band, tells how Ellis Marsalis lent him a baritone, and describes Apollo Theater demands and the station wagon.

segments.chapter: On the road with Guitar Slim
segments.title: Touring by wagon while Slim rode in a Cadillac
segments.summary: The band travelled in a Ford station wagon while Slim arrived by Cadillac, and Ford says Ray Charles drew on Slim.

segments.chapter: On the road with Guitar Slim
segments.title: Guitar Slim's personality and management
segments.summary: Ford describes Slim's drinking, his managers and his modesty about his musicianship.

segments.chapter: On the road with Guitar Slim
segments.title: Slim's showmanship, last records and breaking records on tour
segments.summary: Ford describes Slim walking with his guitar, his late recordings, and the band's success in Florida, Mississippi and Alabama.

segments.chapter: On the road with Guitar Slim
segments.title: Guitar Slim's capo and tuning, and John Lee Hooker
segments.summary: On the new reel Ford explains how Slim used a capo-like key selector rather than retuning, and mentions playing with John Lee Hooker.

segments.title: Being labelled a bebop alto player
segments.summary: After a tape change, Ford says he always wanted to play Dixieland or jazz but was labelled a bebop alto player.

segments.title: Tape change at the fifth reel
segments.summary: A new speaker announces the fifth reel and chat about a party.
